narrative:
The model predicted an 82.7% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors that strongly signaled a high risk of bar exam failure. Your class rank at the end of your first year and your class rank at the end of your third year were the two most influential pieces of information. In both cases you placed in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average ranks of roughly 6th and 5.8th decile seen among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings pushed the prediction heavily toward failure.

Your LSAT score of 28 was the third most important factor. It sits well below the average score of 37 among accepted students and therefore also contributed to the prediction that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed other details such as your middle-income background, 2.2 undergraduate GPA, and plan to attend full-time.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking the LSAT, enrolling in a structured bar-preparation course, or spending time in a post-baccalaureate program that can demonstrably raise your class standing and test skills before reapplying.
